common_name: Chaparral Weeping Mulberry (Fruitless Ornamental Weeping Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted specimen, usually top-worked onto a standard trunk, in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; because Chaparral is a male clone it never fruits, so there is no berry drop or staining to manage beneath the canopy.

directions: Chaparral is a fruitless male selection of white mulberry grown strictly as an ornamental, valued for cascading, gracefully weeping branches clothed in glossy, deeply cut emerald-green leaves that arch to the ground when left untrimmed. Because it produces only small, inconspicuous male catkins and sets no fruit, it is a favorite patio and small-yard tree in Gulf Coast landscapes where homeowners want mulberry foliage texture without the mess of dropped berries. It tolerates heat, drought, urban pollution, and salt spray better than most flowering ornamentals, making it useful along coastal streets and parking areas. Prune annually just above the graft union to shape the weeping canopy and remove any upright shoots that revert toward the rootstock's growth habit.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder
Oregon State University Landscape Plants Database
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant a grafted, top-worked standard in late winter to early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; stake young grafts until the trunk thickens enough to support the weeping, gnarled branch structure on its own.

directions: Named for 19th-century Kansas nurseryman John Teas, this heat-loving dwarf weeping form of white mulberry stays compact at a fraction of the size of a seedling mulberry tree while still bearing a genuine crop of sweet, blackberry-shaped fruit each early summer. The twisted, cascading branches sweep to the ground and give the tree strong winter sculptural interest even when bare of leaves. Fruiting habit and fast growth make it more of a working fruit tree than the strictly ornamental Chaparral clone, so plan for bird pressure and some fruit drop staining beneath the drip line at harvest. It performs reliably in Gulf Coast heat and humidity as long as it has full sun and even soil moisture through fruit development.
sources: Dave Wilson Nursery variety notes
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Kaester is self-fertile and needs no second tree for pollination.

directions: Kaester is a California-origin black mulberry heirloom selected for heavy, reliable cropping of deep purple-to-black fruit roughly an inch long, with a flavor balance that leans more toward sweet than the sharply tart edge found in many black mulberry seedlings. Trees grow into substantial specimens over time and bear over a fairly compact ripening window in midsummer rather than trickling fruit out over many weeks. Because ripe fruit drops and stains hard surfaces heavily, site the tree away from patios and driveways or plan to net and harvest promptly once color develops. Regular deep watering during fruit set improves both fruit size and juice content in hot, dry Gulf Coast summers.
sources: California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Varieties

common_name: Noir de Spain Mulberry (Noir of Spain Black Mulberry)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree (cuttings of Morus nigra root poorly, so nursery stock is typically grafted onto white mulberry rootstock) in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in half to full sun; the cultivar is self-fertile and does not need a second tree.

directions: Noir de Spain is a long-cultivated black mulberry selection prized among fruit collectors for an unusually complex, aromatic flavor that balances sugar and acid more evenly than most other mulberries, with fruit that ripens to a deep red-black rather than the jet black of some other Morus nigra selections. Established trees typically don't bear a full crop until two to three years after planting but then settle into consistent annual production. Because rooted cuttings of true black mulberry are notoriously slow and unreliable, plants sold under this name are almost always grafted, so buy grafted nursery stock rather than attempting to propagate from cuttings at home. Give the tree full sun and consistent moisture through fruit ripening in midsummer, and expect heavy bird interest once fruit begins to color.
sources: Whitman Farms variety notes
One Green World Nursery — Noir de Spain Black Mulberry
California Rare Fruit Growers — Mulberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil with some afternoon shade; leaf color holds best out of the hottest midday sun, and planting a second elderberry cultivar nearby improves fruit set.

directions: This long-grown ornamental sport of American elderberry is grown chiefly for its bright chartreuse-to-gold foliage, which lights up a partly shaded border far more than the plain green leaves of the wild species. Wide, flat-topped clusters of white flowers appear in early summer, followed by small red berries rather than the typical dark purple-black fruit of most Sambucus canadensis selections. In hot Gulf Coast gardens, afternoon shade is important to keep the gold color from scorching to a dull tan by midsummer. Cut back hard in late winter to encourage vigorous new growth with the best foliage color, and remove root suckers regularly to keep the planting from spreading into a colony.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; because flowers and fruit form on the current season's growth, an optional hard cutback (pollard) each winter produces fewer but noticeably larger flower and fruit clusters the following summer.

directions: Maxima is an old selection of American elderberry in which every part of the plant is scaled up from the wild type — the fragrant white flower clusters can reach a foot or more across, and the resulting clusters of purple-black berries are correspondingly larger and heavier than standard wild-collected elderberry. Because flowering wood is produced fresh each year, gardeners willing to cut the whole plant back hard in late winter are rewarded with fewer stems but dramatically oversized flower heads by midsummer; left unpruned, it simply grows into a large multi-stemmed shrub with above-average flower and fruit size. Fruit is used the same way as any American elderberry, for jelly, syrup, and wine, and the plant spreads by suckers over time if not managed. It performs well through Gulf Coast summer heat provided soil moisture stays consistent during flowering and fruit set.
sources: Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with good air movement to reduce fungal pressure on flower and fruit clusters; interplanting with a second elderberry cultivar boosts fruit set.

directions: Samyl was released from the elderberry breeding program at Denmark's Aarslev horticultural research center specifically for commercial juice and cordial production, and it has since been planted commercially across Denmark, Germany, and Sweden. Its main advantage over older European black elderberry selections is an unusually high concentration of anthocyanin pigments in the fruit, which gives pressed juice a deeper color and a sweeter, less astringent flavor than many wild-type black elderberries. Large, flat-topped white flower clusters open in early summer and are themselves used for cordial and syrup before the berries ripen to black in late summer. Because European black elderberry generally prefers cooler, more evenly moist conditions than the Gulf South provides, give this cultivar afternoon shade and supplemental irrigation through summer heat.
sources: Aarhus University — Aarslev Research Centre for Horticulture elderberry breeding program

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; pair with a different elderberry cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and a heavier fruit set.

directions: Sampo is a Danish-bred European black elderberry cultivar developed alongside Samyl for the Scandinavian and Central European processing industry, and researchers studying elderberry juice cultivars have found it produces a distinct anthocyanin pigment profile from Samyl, giving processors two complementary options for blending juice color and flavor. Plants produce the broad, flat clusters of white, fragrant flowers typical of European elderberry in early summer, followed by heavy clusters of small black berries by late summer that are cooked before use, as with all Sambucus nigra fruit. It has been grown commercially in Sweden and Germany in addition to its native Denmark. In Gulf Coast gardens, treat it as a specialty planting rather than a low-maintenance shrub, since it will need afternoon shade and steady soil moisture to get through the region's long, humid summers.
sources: Aarhus University — Aarslev Research Centre for Horticulture elderberry breeding program
